metadata.title: AI agents could threaten banks’ main profit engine

content.text:
Key insight: In a world where AI agents eliminate the friction consumers experience when moving money between accounts, banks could see their net interest margins come under pressure.
What's at stake: The bigger risk of agents for banks may not be runaway agents. It may be agents acting in users' interests.
Last month, Jamie Dimon said that JPMorganChase would not let outside AI agents operate Chase customer accounts. Bank of America, Citi and Schwab followed suit, announcing their own agent crackdowns. Amazon is trying to block agents too, suing to keep Perplexity's shopping agent out of customer accounts, and seeking to block Meta's Muse personal agent.
This surge in action from banks and e-commerce is driven by fears of thousands of AIs running amok, or the idea that "rogue agents" will take actions beyond users' intentions. Banks are right to be concerned: Agents with customer credentials pose security risks and can make mistakes that users themselves end up paying for.
However, the bigger risk of agents for banks may not be runaway agents. It may be agents acting in users' interests.
Most significantly, agents are likely to generate more competition for deposits. This could happen if agents make it easier for users to move their money from low-yield savings accounts at legacy banks to accounts with higher interest rates. Moving money today means checking NerdWallet, potentially creating a new bank account or navigating a portal to buy a money market fund. That friction is enough to stop more money from moving into higher yielding accounts today. An agent that monitors rates and moves the funds to the highest FDIC insured account could easily overcome that stickiness.
The stakes are high. The FDIC reports that banks hold more than $4 trillion in non-interest bearing deposits. Trillions more are near zero percent. Altogether, the average rate banks pay on customer deposits is less than 0.1% on checking accounts and 0.38% on savings accounts, while fintechs offer up to 4.4%.
Banks' 3.3% net interest margin is the most significant driver of bank income, accounting for 40%-50% of large bank operating income and 60%-70% of smaller bank operating income according to the Kansas City Fed. Yield-seeking agents could significantly cut into those margins.
It's also worth spelling out how banks use deposits and long-term lending to stay solvent — and how challenges to the "deposit franchise" could destabilize banks. When the Federal Reserve raises interest rates, banks make more money from deposits, because they can earn higher market rates on reserves and new loans they make — but don't significantly change the interest rate on your savings or checking account. At the same time, the value of the mortgages and loans to businesses that they hold tends to go down, especially when long-term Treasury yields go up. These two effects roughly cancel out … unless the deposits leave.
How big could the hit be to bank earnings? McKinsey found that agent-driven competition for deposits could reduce bank profits from deposits by as much as 37%. And the Financial Times' John Foley estimates that a major hit to interest income could cost banks as much as 10% of their equity valuations, a hit of $500 billion, based on the decline in future cash flows.
And if banks don't pay higher rates on deposits, they risk some form of what Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok described as an "agentic bank run." This could happen quite quickly, especially if there are signs of trouble at a bank. (Think a Silicon Valley Bank group chat-driven run at 1,000 times speed). In the bank-run circumstance, the agent is likely "aligned" with the customer at the individual level, but in aggregate, they cause big problems for the bank, its customers and the FDIC.
Banks depend on other kinds of frictions as well. For instance, two thirds of buyers apply to just one lender for their mortgage, often because most borrowers rely heavily on lenders and brokers themselves for information about mortgages, despite research showing that shopping around can save up to $1,200. On credit cards, issuers make money largely from the borrowers' revolving monthly balances and late fees. Credit cards in particular compensate sophisticated borrowers at the expense of less sophisticated borrowers.
While bankers' interests in bank earnings are clear, why should the rest of us care? This question demands deeper consideration given that most of the challenges to bank earnings that we've discussed produce savings or more money for consumers. But the core challenge is that these hits to banks' business models and profitability could create serious stability problems. An IMF study found that lower bank profits are associated with higher systemic risk and that banks relying heavily on non-interest income contributes to higher risk as well.
To be sure, AI brings significant potential upside for banks: from the significant borrowing we're seeing already to finance the AI build-out to the potential for more transactions from agentic commerce. But facing a new era of AI agents, banks and bank regulators will face two sources of risk: The first is agents slowly bidding up rates and reducing profits from other frictions; the second is the potential for agents to move money out of banks very quickly, risking bank runs.
In many ways, consumers having the power to easily get higher rates is a positive development that policymakers and banks should welcome. But this competition will very likely force banks to find new business models that depend less on friction. The critical balancing act for banks and regulators will be leaning into the positives of this new world while ensuring bank stability and the continued availability of lending.
One step banks can take in the short term is developing systems to circuit-break large-scale bank runs led by agents. Banks could partner with developers to build in guardrails into the agents that banks do let in — including short delays on agent-driven withdrawals.
Banking with less friction is very likely in our future. Bankers and policymakers alike will need to lean into policies and systems that embrace what will hopefully be a new era of competition, consumer surplus, and stability that Americans can count on.
